spots.look: Oil should be at the bottom of the fill hole. Metal flakes or a burnt smell mean wear.

find: Note the noise: a whine that changes on and off the gas = ring and pinion gears. A rumble that changes with turning = bearings. A clunk = backlash or U-joint.
Check the fluid: remove the fill plug. Fluid should come right to the bottom edge of the hole.
Look for leaks at the cover, pinion seal and axle ends.
Check the magnet on the drain plug or inside the cover for metal. A little fine fuzz is normal; chunks are not.
fix: Fill to the bottom of the fill hole with the right gear oil.
Change the fluid: drain, clean the cover, reseal with a new gasket or gasket maker, refill.
Replace a leaking pinion seal (mark the nut position; preload matters). Axle seals are medium DIY.
Whining gears or worn bearings need a differential rebuild by a driveline shop.

death_wobble.safety: Death wobble is dangerous. When it starts, slow down firmly without slamming the brakes, and keep a tight grip. Do not drive at highway speed until it is fixed.

spots.name: Track bar
spots.where: A bar from the axle to the frame across the front (solid axle trucks and Jeeps).
spots.look: Movement at the ends or bushings when the steering wheel is rocked; loose bolts; cracked bracket.

spots.name: Ball joints
spots.where: Steering knuckles.
spots.look: Play when rocking the tire top to bottom.

spots.name: Tie rods and drag link
spots.where: Steering linkage across the front axle.
spots.look: Any slop in the ends.

spots.name: Steering box mount
spots.where: Where the steering gear bolts to the frame.
spots.look: Cracks or movement at the frame.

spots.name: Steering stabilizer
spots.where: A shock across the steering.
spots.look: A worn one hides the problem but does not cause it.

find: Have a helper rock the steering wheel side to side quickly (engine running, parked) while you watch every steering joint from under the front. Look for any movement other than turning.
Track bar first: watch both ends. Any clunk or play there is the most common cause.
Jack up each front wheel and check ball joints (top/bottom rock) and tie rods (side to side rock).
Check the torque on the track bar and control arm bolts.
Check tire balance and caster after a lift.
fix: Tighten loose bolts to spec. Replace any worn track bar, ends, ball joints or tie rods.
Lifted trucks: an adjustable track bar and a caster correction may be needed.
Balance the tires and set the pressure right.
Replace the steering stabilizer only after the real cause is fixed.
Check your VIN for recalls (Jeep had a track bar bracket recall).

air_suspension_problem.safety: Never get under a vehicle supported only by air suspension. Use jack stands, and put the system in service or jack mode if it has one.

spots.name: Air springs (bags)
spots.where: At each corner where a coil spring would be.
spots.look: Cracks in the rubber, especially at the folds, or a corner sitting low after parking.

spots.name: Compressor
spots.where: Usually under the front or rear of the vehicle.
spots.look: Running a long time or often, very hot, or not running at all.

spots.name: Air lines and fittings
spots.where: Small plastic tubes to each corner.
spots.look: Rubbed or cracked lines, loose fittings.

find: Note which corner sags after sitting overnight. That corner has the leak.
Spray soapy water on that air spring, its fitting and line. Bubbles show the leak.
Listen for the compressor. Running a long time or often means a leak; never running means a fuse, relay or failed compressor.
Read the suspension codes with a capable scan tool.
fix: Replace a leaking air spring (often 2 bolts and a line fitting, with the corner supported).
Replace or reconnect a leaking line.
Replace a bad relay or compressor. A failing compressor is often caused by a leak making it overwork; fix the leak too.
Some owners convert to coil springs; that changes how it rides and turns on a warning on some vehicles.

blend_door_actuator.safety: Disconnect the battery if you are unplugging connectors behind the dash.

spots.name: Blend door actuator
spots.where: A small plastic motor on the side of the heater box under the dash (passenger side or center on many trucks).
spots.look: Clicking or tapping from behind the dash, especially after starting or changing temperature.

spots.name: Heater hoses
spots.where: Firewall.
spots.look: Both hot with the heater on = the core is fine and the door is the problem.

find: Symptoms: clicking behind the dash, temperature stuck hot or cold, or one side hot and one cold on dual-zone systems.
Feel both heater hoses at the firewall with the engine warm. If both are hot and the air is still cold, the blend door is not moving.
Listen behind the dash while changing the temperature to find which actuator clicks.
On many GMs, unplugging the battery for 10 minutes then letting it recalibrate (do not touch the controls for 1 minute after starting) fixes a confused actuator.
fix: Try the recalibration first (battery off, then let it sit after starting).
Remove the lower dash panel or glove box to reach the actuator.
Unplug it, remove the 2 or 3 screws, and install the new one. Plug it in before screwing it down so it can find its position.
Turn the key on and let it calibrate before using the controls.

instrument_cluster_problem.safety: Disconnect the battery before removing the cluster. Do not drive without a working speedometer.

spots.name: Gauge cluster
spots.where: Behind the dash bezel in front of the driver.
spots.look: Gauges stuck, dead or jumping. GM trucks 2003 to 2006 are known for failing gauge stepper motors.

spots.name: Fuses and grounds
spots.where: Fuse box and behind the dash.
spots.look: A blown cluster fuse or a loose ground causes the whole cluster to act up.

find: Note which gauges fail: one gauge stuck = that stepper motor. All dead = fuse, ground, or the cluster itself.
Many GM clusters have a self-test: with the key off, hold the trip/odometer button and turn the key on. All needles should sweep.
Check the cluster fuse.
If the speedometer and the transmission both act up, check the vehicle speed sensor instead.
fix: Replace a blown fuse or fix a loose ground.
Remove the dash bezel and the cluster (several screws and a connector).
Send it to a cluster repair service or replace the stepper motors (requires soldering).
A replacement cluster may need the mileage programmed; repair services usually keep your mileage.

infotainment_problem.safety: Do not try to fix it while driving.

spots.name: Screen and radio
spots.where: Center of the dash.
spots.look: Freezing, rebooting, black screen, or no sound.

spots.name: Radio fuse
spots.where: Fuse box.
spots.look: Blown or a loose fuse.

find: Try a soft reset: on many vehicles hold the power button 10 to 20 seconds until it restarts.
Forget the vehicle on your phone and pair it again. Update your phone.
Check for a software update from the maker (many can be installed at home with a USB stick or over the air).
Try a different USB cable for CarPlay or Android Auto; bad cables cause most disconnects.
If it is completely dead, check the radio fuse.
fix: Do the reset, re-pair, and update.
Pull the radio fuse for 1 minute (radio off) to force a full reset.
Ask the dealer about software bulletins; many screen problems are fixed by updates.
A failed head unit can be replaced; aftermarket units may need an adapter to keep steering wheel controls.

window_regulator_problem.safety: Tape the glass up so it cannot fall when you unbolt it. Keep fingers away from the regulator; it can snap.

spots.name: Window switch
spots.where: Door panel or center console.
spots.look: Try the window from both the driver master switch and its own switch.

spots.name: Motor and regulator
spots.where: Inside the door behind the panel.
spots.look: Grinding or crunching, a window that drops, goes crooked, or the motor running with no movement.

spots.name: Door wiring
spots.where: The rubber boot between the door and the body.
spots.look: Broken wires from opening and closing the door.

find: Press the switch and listen. Motor runs but window does not move = broken regulator (cable or gear). No sound = switch, wiring or motor.
Try the other switch (driver master or the door's own).
With the panel off, check for power at the motor plug when pressing the switch. Power but no movement = bad motor.
Check the wiring in the door hinge boot for broken wires.
fix: Remove the door panel (screws in the armrest and handle, then pop the clips).
Peel back the plastic weather sheet carefully.
Tape the window up in the closed position.
Unbolt the glass from the regulator, unbolt the regulator and motor, and remove through the access hole.
Install the new assembly, bolt the glass on, test before putting the panel back.

tools: Spray lubricant (white lithium grease or silicone)
door_lock_problem.safety: Disconnect the battery if you unplug the airbag or side impact sensors in some doors.

spots.name: Key fob
spots.where: Your key.
spots.look: Weak battery, or only one door not working (fob is fine then).

spots.name: Door lock actuator
spots.where: Inside the door at the latch.
spots.look: Buzzing or a weak click with no lock movement.

spots.name: Door wiring
spots.where: Rubber boot between door and body.
spots.look: Broken wires.

find: If no doors respond to the fob, replace the fob battery and try the door switch inside.
If only one door will not lock, that door's actuator or wiring is the likely problem.
Listen at the door when pressing lock. A buzz or weak click = worn actuator.
Check the lock fuse if no doors work from any switch.
fix: Replace the fob battery.
Spray lubricant into the latch and work it.
Replace the door lock actuator: remove the door panel, disconnect the rods and plug, unbolt the latch (often 3 Torx screws on the door edge), and swap.
Repair broken wires in the door hinge boot.

tools: Compressed air or trimmer line to clear drains
water_leak_inside.safety: A wet carpet grows mold and can damage wiring and airbag modules under the seats. Dry it out quickly.

spots.name: A/C drain
spots.where: A rubber tube through the firewall, usually passenger side, that drips under the truck.
spots.look: No drip under the truck with A/C running and a wet passenger floor = plugged drain.

spots.name: Cowl and windshield
spots.where: Base of the windshield.
spots.look: Clogged leaves in the cowl, or a bad windshield seal.

spots.name: Door seals
spots.where: Rubber seals around the doors.
spots.look: Torn, flattened or loose seals.

spots.name: Third brake light and roof
spots.where: Top of the cab.
spots.look: Water stains on the headliner below it. Very common on pickup trucks.

spots.name: Sunroof drains
spots.where: Tubes at the corners of the sunroof.
spots.look: Clogged drains overflow into the headliner.

find: Find where the water ends up: front floor, rear floor, headliner or trunk.
Have a helper sit inside with a flashlight while you run a garden hose slowly over one area at a time, starting low and moving up. Give each spot a few minutes.
With the A/C running on a humid day, look for a drip under the passenger side. No drip and a wet floor = plugged drain.
Clear leaves from the cowl at the base of the windshield.
Check the third brake light gasket on pickups if water is in the headliner.
fix: Unclog the A/C drain by gently pushing a trimmer line into it or a short puff of compressed air.
Clean the cowl and sunroof drains.
Reseal the third brake light or roof marker lights with a new gasket.
Replace torn door seals.
Pull back the carpet and dry the padding completely with a wet/dry vac and fans.

tools: Screwdriver or small hammer to probe rust
rust_damage.safety: Rusted brake lines, fuel lines or frames are a safety problem. Have frame rust checked by a shop before driving at speed or towing.

spots.name: Frame
spots.where: Main rails under the truck, especially above the rear axle and near the spring hangers.
spots.look: Flaking layers, holes, or rust that a screwdriver pokes through.

spots.name: Brake and fuel lines
spots.where: Along the frame rails.
spots.look: Swollen or flaking lines. GM trucks of the 2000s commonly rust brake lines.

spots.name: Rocker panels and cab corners
spots.where: Under the doors and the lower back corners of the cab.
spots.look: Bubbling paint or holes. Common on 1999 to 2007 GM trucks.

spots.name: Wheel wells
spots.where: Fender lips.
spots.look: Bubbling paint.

find: Get under the truck with a good flashlight. Tap suspect areas with a hammer or poke with a screwdriver. Solid metal rings; rotten metal crunches or goes through.
Follow the brake and fuel lines and look for swollen, flaking spots.
Look at rocker panels and cab corners. Push on bubbling paint.
Check where the suspension mounts to the frame. Rust there matters most.
fix: Surface rust: wire brush it, use a rust converter, then paint or undercoat.
Replace rusted brake lines right away.
Rocker and cab corner patch panels are welded in. A body shop job unless you weld.
Frame rot near suspension mounts may need a frame section or a frame replacement. Get a shop's opinion.
Wash the underside in winter in salt states.

adas_problem.safety: Driver assist systems help but do not replace you. If they act up, turn them off in the settings and drive normally until fixed.

spots.name: Front radar
spots.where: Behind the grille emblem or lower bumper.
spots.look: Mud, snow, ice or bugs covering it, or a bumper that was hit.

spots.name: Windshield camera
spots.where: At the top center of the windshield behind the mirror.
spots.look: Dirt, fog, or a crack in front of it. A new windshield needs calibration.

spots.name: Bumper sensors
spots.where: Small round sensors on the bumpers, and rear corner radars for blind spot.
spots.look: Dirt or damage.

find: Read the message on the dash; it often says which sensor is blocked.
Clean the grille emblem, bumper sensors and the windshield in front of the camera.
Note if it started after a windshield replacement, a front bumper repair, or an alignment.
Write down when false braking or lane alerts happen (bridges, shadows) for the dealer.
Look up your VIN for recalls on automatic emergency braking.
fix: Keep sensors clean, especially in winter.
After a windshield or bumper repair, have the camera and radar calibrated (static or dynamic calibration at a dealer or glass shop).
Get software updates from the dealer.
Replace damaged sensors.
